Abstract
Background  Species delimitation within Camellia sect. Thea is taxonomically challenging due to its complex 
evolutionary history. This study aims to utilize nuclear and chloroplast data as genomic DNA barcodes to delimit 
species within this economically important group of plants.
Results  Whole genome sequencing (WGS) data were obtained for 98 accessions representing all but one species in 
C. sect. Thea. Based on 759 high-quality SCNs, 98 whole chloroplast genomes, and by using 2× coverage clean reads 
from WGS for Skmer analyses, we found that combining the findings from these three data sets resulted in nearly 
complete species delimitation and resolution of all interspecific relationships within C. sect. Thea. We also found 
support for the taxonomic elevation of two varieties (C. sinensis var. assamica and C. tachangensis var. remotiserrata) 
to species status (C. assamica and C. remotiserrata, respectively). Furthermore, we confirmed that C. formosensis 
represents a distinct species. Gene tree discordances, chloroplast-nuclear conflicts and complex network-like 
phylogenetic relationships were observed in C. sect. Thea.
Conclusion  Compared with the use of single parentally inherited chloroplast data sources, utilizing both 
uniparentally inherited chloroplast data and biparentally inherited nuclear data improved the species delimitation 
of taxa within C. sect. Thea. The intricate phylogenetic relationships observed are likely a result of widespread past 
hybridization and chloroplast capture events among species within this group, which may have blurred the species 
boundaries. Our novel approach to species delimitation within C. sect. Thea may serve as a blueprint for employing 
genomic DNA barcodes in other taxa with complex histories, and will significantly contribute to the conservation of 
cultivated tea plant species and their wild relatives.

Introduction
Species within Camellia sect. Thea (L.) Dyer (Theaceae), 
including the economically important C. sinensis (L.) 
Kuntze and its wild relatives are cultivated for their sec­
ondary metabolites, which contribute to the unique fla­
vor and health benefits of tea [1]. This section comprises 
approximately 12 species that are native to southern 
China, NE India, Myanmar, Laos, Vietnam, and Thai­
land [2]. Notably, species such as C. crassicolumna Hung 
T. Chang, C. ptilophylla Hung T. Chang, C. sinensis, C. 
tachangensis F. S. Zhang and C. taliensis (W. W. Sm.) 
Melch. are important economic crops for tea breeding 
and production in China and neighboring countries [3–
7]. Camellia sinensis is the most valuable crop, and it has 
a domestication history spanning more than 3,000 years 
[8]. Its two varieties, C. sinensis var. sinensis and C. sinen­
sis var. assamica (J. W. Masters) Kitamura, are cultivated 
in more than 60 countries for beverage tea production 
[9]. Compared with the two widely cultivated tea variet­
ies, several C. sect. Thea species (i.e., C. crassicolumna, C. 
costata Hu & S. Ye Liang, C. gymnogyna Hung T. Chang, 
C. ptilophylla, and C. taliensis) have attracted significant 
attention for breeding low-caffeine tea plants, as their 
lower caffeine content may be beneficial to human health 
[7, 10, 11]. These species thus represent a vital genetic 
resource for future breeding programs in the global tea 
industry [12–15].
However, the taxonomy of C. sect. Thea has long been 
debated, largely because of overlapping morphological 
variation and geographic distribution among species. For 
example, a total of 32 species and four varieties in the sec­
tion were recognized by Chang and Ren [16], whereas 12 
species and six varieties were defined by Ming [17]. Many 
taxa of the former classification system were treated as 
synonyms of species or as varieties in the latter and in the 
Flora of China [17]. For instance, C. danzaiensis Chang 
& K. M. Lan, C. kwangtungensis Hung T. Chang, and 
C. yungkiangensis Hung T. Chang were treated as syn­
onyms of C. costata Hu & S. Ye Liang; likewise, C. dehu­
ngensis Hung T. Chang & B. H. Chen and C. assamica (J. 
W. Mast.) Hung T. Chang were treated as varieties of C. 
sinensis [17, 18]. Later, C. formosensis (Masam. & Suzuki) 
M. H. Su, C. F. Hsieh & C. H. Tsou was raised to species 
level [19]. Others were newly described, such as C. sinen­
sis var. dulcamara Q. U. Le & Nguyen and C. sinensis var. 
madoensis T.V. Nguyen, V. D. Luong & N. Trieu Le [20, 
21]. Thus, the taxonomy and species delimitation of C. 
sect. Thea remains in flux and needs to be addressed.
Morphological similarities among Camellia spe­
cies often complicate species identification. Frequent 
gene flow and introgression among sympatric species 
in Camellia [12, 22–24], along with continuous mor­
phological variation resulting from artificial hybrid 
breeding programs [10, 25], pose challenges for species 
identification by morphology within this genus, espe­
cially in C. sect. Thea [26, 27]. Recent studies have dem­
onstrated that chloroplast genomes show promise in 
phylogenetic reconstruction of Theaceae and Camel­
lia [28–31]. However, these studies have generally suf­
fered from limited sampling within C. sect. Thea, which 
restricts our understanding of the species boundaries 
in this section. A more recent study [32], which incor­
porated a broader sampling of C. sect. Thea, employed 
chloroplast genomes to assess species delimitation under 
Chang and Ren’s classification [16]. Their findings suggest 
that many morphospecies recognized in Chang’s classifi­
cation system were not supported by chloroplast genome 
data, suggesting that the chloroplast genome alone can­
not effectively delineate species or that some morphospe­
cies may be too narrowly defined. Despite the improved 
sampling [32], this study did not incorporate nuclear 
genomic data, leaving a gap in the evaluation of species 
boundaries and highlighting the need for a more integra­
tive genomic approach.
Genome skimming data has commonly been used to 
obtain the chloroplast genome in Camellia and other 
taxa of Theaceae [30, 33]. To include nuclear sequence 
information contained within genome skimming data, 
assembly-free methods have been developed to estimate 
genetic distances among species for species delimitation. 
One promising method is the Skmer analysis [34], which 
utilizes low-coverage genome skimming data for phyloge­
netic tree construction based on genetic distances among 
species and has shown effectiveness in species delimita­
tion in several genera, such as Cymbidium, Schima, and 
Torreya [35–37]. However, its application for species dis­
crimination within C. sect. Thea has remained untested. 
Furthermore, while some studies have attempted to 
assemble single-copy nuclear genes from genome skim­
ming [38, 39], deeper sequencing has been shown to yield 
a greater number of single-copy nuclear orthologous 
genes (SCNs) [40]. SCNs assembled from the transcrip­
tome or whole-genome sequencing (WGS) have been 
effectively used in Theaceae and Camellia phylogenomic 
studies [1, 22, 41]. For instance, the phylogenetic rela­
tionships within Camellia were well resolved on the basis 
of 405 low-copy nuclear genes assembled from transcrip­
tome data [1]. However, owing to the limited sampling 
of only one individual per species, species delimitation 
could not be evaluated in these studies. Consequently, 
the efficacy of Skmer and SCNs for species delimitation 
with multiple individuals sampled per species within C. 
sect. Thea has not yet been explored.
In this study, we sampled a total of 98 accessions, with 
multiple samples per species representing all 12 spe­
cies within C. sect. Thea as defined by Ming [17] (except 
for C. sealyama T. L. Ming, which is endemic to Laos) 
to investigate species delimitation via chloroplast and

nuclear genomic DNA barcodes. Specifically, focusing on 
two primary tea plant varieties, C. sinensis var. sinensis 
and C. sinensis var. assamica, we collected samples from 
ancient tea trees that were considered to be the clos­
est relatives to wild plants and ancient landraces, since 
no true wild populations could be traced. Our objec­
tives were to address the following questions: (1) Can 
C. sect. Thea species be accurately delimitated via inte­
grating chloroplast and nuclear genomic data? (2) If spe­
cies delimitation is unsuccessful, what factors may have 
contributed to the failure of species delimitation? The 
findings here will make a significant contribution to the 
taxonomy of C. sect. Thea and inform conservation and 
help its sustainable utilization as tea plant germplasm in 
future breeding programs.
Materials and methods
Plant materials
We sampled a total of 98 accessions (Table S1), compris­
ing 97 samples from C. sect. Thea and one outgroup, rep­
resenting all 12 currently recognized species of C. sect. 
Thea following Ming (except C. sealyama) [17]. Among 
the samples, a wild tea tree referred to as C. sinensis 
‘DASZ’, for which a genome has been assembled [42], 
was included to check its identity. For each taxon (except 
C. sinensis var. sinensis and C. sinensis var. assamica) of 
C. sect. Thea, two to ten accessions were collected from 
wild populations. Specifically, for the two principal culti­
vated varieties, C. sinensis var. sinensis and C. sinensis var. 
assamica, we sampled a total of 20 and 29 individuals, 
respectively, including ancient tea trees, ancient landra­
ces, and modern cultivars across their entire distribution 
range, to encompass the diversity within the two varieties 
(Table S1). The outgroup Pyrenaria oblongicarpa Hung 
T. Chang from outside Camellia was selected based on 
previous studies [22, 43]. The geographic distribution of 
the 98 accessions from C. sect. Thea used in this study 
is illustrated in Fig. S1. Comprehensive information, 
including the individual who undertook the formal iden­
tification of the plant material, can be found in Table S1.
Genomic DNA extraction and WGS data acquisition
For WGS, fresh, healthy leaves were collected and imme­
diately dried in silica gel for subsequent total genomic 
DNA extraction by a modified CTAB method [44]. Total 
DNA was quantified via a Qubit instrument (Invitro­
gen) and sheared into approximately 500  bp fragments 
for Illumina library construction, following standard 
protocols (NEBNext® Ultra IITM DNA Library Prep 
Kit for Illumina®). WGS was conducted on an Illumina 
NovaSeq 6000 (San Diego, USA) platform with 150  bp 
paired-end reads at Novogene (Beijing, China). WGS 
data were newly acquired for 89 out of the 98 accessions 
in this study, whereas the raw data for the remaining nine 
samples [42, 45–47] were obtained from GenBank (Table 
S1).
Assembly of SCNs and chloroplast genomes
The raw WGS data were filtered with Fastp v.0.20.1 for 
base correction and reads where more than 40% of the 
bases had a Phred quality of less than 20 were removed 
[48]. These filtered data were then utilized to assemble 
the SCNs. Initially, a reference sequence file was prepared 
with a Hyb-Seq script [49] based on 33,021 protein-
coding genes (CDSs) from the reference genome of the 
ancient tea tree DASZ (National Genomics Data Cen­
ter BioProject number: PRJCA002039). Subsequently, 
Orthofinder v.2.5.2 [50] was employed to identify poten­
tial orthologous genes via protein-coding sequences from 
six tea plant genomes as input files: C. sinensis var. assa­
mica ‘Yunkang10’ (PRJNA381277), C. sinensis ‘DASZ’ 
(PRJCA002039), C. sinensis ‘Biyun11’ (PRJCA002071), 
C. sinensis var. sinensis ‘Longjing43’ (PRJCA001158), C. 
sinensis var. sinensis ‘Tieguanyin’ (PRJNA665594), and 
another C. sinensis var. sinensis (PRJCA001305). Finally, 
the SCNs identified by both Hyb-Seq and Orthofinder 
were used as reference sequences to assemble each indi­
vidual SCN with HybPiper v.2.0 [51]. To obtain a high-
quality SCN dataset, each candidate SCN with sequences 
longer than 50% of the reference and present in more 
than 90% of the total 98 samples was retained. Each set 
of SCN gene sequences was subsequently aligned using 
MAFFT v.7.490 [52] with default parameter settings. 
Then, poorly aligned sites were trimmed via Gblocks 
v.0.91b with the parameter ‘-b5 = h’ [53]. Geneious v.9.0.2 
[54] was used to manually check the alignments, and the 
beginnings and ends that were rich in gaps were manu­
ally trimmed, resulting in a final dataset comprising 759 
core SCNs designated the “98taxa-SCN” dataset.
Chloroplast genome assembly for the 98 accessions 
via WGS data was carried out with GetOrangelle v.1.7.5 
[55] with default settings. The annotation of the chlo­
roplast genomes was carried out with PGA [56], using 
the chloroplast genome of C. parvisepala Hung T. 
Chang (NC_058924) as a reference. They were manually 
checked for start and end codons of the coding regions 
in Geneious v.9.0.2 [54]. The 98 newly assembled chlo­
roplast genomes were designated the “98taxa-pt” dataset 
and deposited in GenBank with the accession numbers 
provided in Table S1.
Phylogenetic analysis
To evaluate the efficacy of species delimitation, we 
employed a tree-based method utilizing concatenated 
datasets of chloroplast genomes (98taxa-pt) and 759 
SCNs (98taxa-SCN) to reconstruct phylogenetic trees. 
AMAS v.1.0 [57] was used to concatenate the align­
ments of the 759 SCNs, whereas maximum likelihood

default settings, with automated model selection and 
1,000 replicates of SH-aLRT single-branch tests and 
1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates for both chloroplast 
and nuclear datasets. RAxML v.8.2.12 [59] was also used 
on both datasets with the GTRGAMMA model and the

rapid bootstrap (BS) replicates. For successful species 
delimitation based on phylogenetic trees, a species/vari­
ety was considered to be successfully delineated when all 
conspecific individuals were resolved as monophyletic 
[60].
Skmer analysis
Skmer v.3.3.0 is an assembly-free and alignment-free 
tool to compute genomic distances between the query 
and reference genome skims and shows high accuracy 
in estimating distances and identifying the closest match 
in reference datasets [34]. We employed this method to 
calculate genomic distances using cleaned WGS data 
with approximately 2× coverage (~ 6 Gb) to reconstruct 
a distance tree using default parameters (​h​t​t​p​s​:​/​/​g​i​t​h​u​b​.​c​
o​m​/​s​h​a​h​a​b​-​s​a​r​m​a​s​h​g​h​i​/​S​k​m​e​r) after the chloroplast and 
mitochondrial reads were excluded [35].
Phylogenetic discordance and network analysis
To explore phylogenetic (dis)concordances among gene 
trees relative to the concatenated tree generated by IQ-
Tree, we employed Phyparts v.0.0.1 [61] with a bootstrap 
support cut-off of 50%. All 759 gene trees were rooted 
with the outgroup P. oblongicarpa via Newick [62] before 
comparison with the concatenated SCN tree. The results 
were visualized using the script phypartspiecharts.py (​h​t​t​
p​s​:​/​/​g​i​t​h​u​b​.​c​o​m​/​m​o​s​s​m​a​t​t​e​r​s​/​p​h​y​l​o​s​c​r​i​p​t​s​/).
Camellia is a rapidly radiating genus [63] with several 
species of known interspecific hybrid origin [22–24]. 
Thus, bifurcating phylogenetic trees may inadequately 
represent these complex evolutionary relationships. We 
employed a split network approach to investigate the 
reticulate relationships among C. sect. Thea species on 
the basis of concatenated nuclear sequences from the 
98taxa-SCN dataset. This method visualizes complex 
evolutionary relationships through cross-connections 
between branches in a phylogenetic network [64]. This 
analysis was implemented in SplitsTree v.5.3.0 [65] based 
on P distances and the neighbor-net al.gorithm [64].
Results
Chloroplast genome and SCN assembly
The coverage depth of the WGS data for the 89 newly 
sequenced accessions ranged from 13× to 27×. The data 
for the remaining nine WGS accessions downloaded from 
previously released data had coverages ranging from 11× 
to 21×. Consistent with the previous release of Camellia 
chloroplast genomes, all 98 newly generated plastomes in 
this study presented a quadripartite structure, compris­
ing a large single copy (LSC), a small single copy (SSC) 
and two inverted repeats (IRa and IRb), with genome 
sizes ranging from 155,699 to 157,170  bp (Table S1). 
The lengths of the LSC, SSC and IR regions varied from 
86,055 to 86,704 bp, 16,877 to 18,363 bp, and 25,961 to 
26,111 bp, respectively. Excluding one duplicated IR, the 
chloroplast genomes of all the C. sect. Thea accessions 
had 115 unique genes, including 81 protein-coding, 30 
tRNA and four rRNA genes. Among these genes, 12 pro­
tein-coding genes and six tRNA genes contained introns. 
The length of the 98taxa-pt matrix was 132,105 bp, with 
1,483 parsimony-informative (PI) sites (1.12%).
A total of 7,373 nuclear genes were identified from 
33,021 CDS as putative single-copy genes via Hyb-seq, 
whereas 3,372 genes were identified as SCNs from six 
genomes via OrthoFinder. Among these genes, 1,344 
genes were shared between both methods and were 
retained as reference genes for SCN assembly. Ultimately, 
a total of 759 high-quality SCNs met our filtering crite­
ria. The lengths of these core SCNs ranged from 662 to 
5615 bp and had a concatenated length of 1,253,839 bp 
with 73,832 PI sites (5.89%).
Phylogenetic relationships of plastomes, 759 SCNs, and 
Skmer analyses
The topologies of the phylogenetic trees were highly 
consistent between the two ML trees reconstructed by 
RAxML and IQ-Tree, the Skmer and SCNs trees (Fig. 1; 
Fig. S2). All phylogenies revealed that samples of C. sect. 
Thea clustered into two major clades (pt - I/S-I/C - I and 
pt - II/S-II/C - II). Some incongruences between the 
Skmer and concatenated 98taxa-SCN trees were appar­
ent (Fig. 1): e.g., the position of sample C. fangchengen­
sis re378, which was in a basal grade with C. sinensis var. 
lasiocalyx samples in the former and a near-basal grade in 
clade N-II in the latter; and the position of C. grandibrac­
teata samples, which were nested among the C. sinensis 
var. assamica samples in the former and were sister to 
all C. sinensis var. assamica samples in the latter. Strong 
phylogenetic discordances were also apparent between 
the chloroplast and nuclear trees for certain individuals 
of several species (e.g., C. fangchengensis, C. gymnogyna, 
C. leptophylla, C. ptilophylla and C. sinensis var. assam­
ica) (Fig. 1; Fig. S2). Notably, the ancient tea tree ‘DASZ’ 
was positioned as the sister branch to all other species in 
clades S-II and N-II of the nuclear trees but was nested 
within the C. taliensis clade (clade pt-I; BS: 87 & 83%) in 
the plastome trees (Fig. 1; Fig. S2).
In the plastome tree, C. crassicolumna, C. kwangsien­
sis, C. sinensis var. lasiocalyx, C. taliensis, C. tachangensis 
var. tachangensis, C. sinensis ‘DASZ’, and seven acces­
sions of C. sinensis var. assamica formed the maximally

Species delimitation based on Chloroplast and nuclear 
data
Our study strongly supported the monophyly of six taxa 
in both the chloroplast and nuclear trees: C. costata, C. 
formosensis, C. leptophylla, C. ptilophylla, C. tachangensis 
var. remotiserrata, and C. tachangensis var. tachangensis 
(Fig. 1; Table 1). Notably, all monophylies were supported 
with a bootstrap value of 100% in both datasets, except 
for C. tachangensis var. tachangensis, which exhibited 
moderate support (BS = 68%) in the SCN tree. Interest­
ingly, the monophyly of C. kwangsiensis was highly sup­
ported in both the chloroplast and the Skmer trees (BS: 
99–100%), but one sample of C. crassicolumna clustered 
within this clade in the SCN tree (Fig. 1). In addition, the 
monophyly of C. sinensis var. assamica was highly sup­
ported in the SCN trees (BS: 99%), but it exhibited dis­
crepancies in both the chloroplast and the Skmer trees 
(Fig. 1). The samples of C. tachangensis var. remotiserrata 
formed a distinct clade separate from those of C. tachan­
gensis var. tachangensis in both the chloroplast and 
nuclear trees. Two species, C. fangchengensis and C. gym­
nogyna, were monophyletic in the chloroplast trees (both

clade with the C. tachangensis var. tachangensis samples 
nesting within it, with high support (BS: 100%) (Fig.  1; 
Fig. S2B). Conversely, while the monophyly of both C. 
grandibracteata and C. taliensis was strongly supported

Discussion
Species delimitation within Camellia sect. Thea
Discrepancies in species delimitation within C. sect. 
Thea was associated with the type of data and methods 
employed. All three data sets (i.e., plastid genome, 759 
SCNs and 2× coverage clean WGS reads) provided the 
same level of discrimination power but recovered differ­
ent taxa (Table 1). For instance, C. sinensis var. assamica 
was only delimited by SCNs. In contrast, C. kwangsiensis 
was delimitated by nuclear Skmer analyses and chloro­
plast data, and C. fangchengensis and C. gymnogyna were 
delimitated by chloroplast only. Six taxa within C. sect. 
Thea (C. costata, C. formosensis, C. leptophylla, C. ptilo­
phylla, C. tachangensis var. remotiserrata, and C. tachan­
gensis var. tachangensis) were consistently delimited with 
all three data sets, though only two or three samples per 
taxon were included. More samples need to be included 
in future studies to confirm our findings here. Our find­
ings specifically supported the distinct species status of 
C. tachangensis var. remotiserrata, C. remotiserrata H. T. 
Chang [16, 66], rather than being a variety of C. tachan­
gensis as previously suggested by Ming [17]. Overall, our 
species delineation resulted in high support (99–100%) 
in one or the other data set, nuclear or chloroplast. Col­
lectively, our results underscore the advantage of using 
different data types, and multiple samples per taxon, to 
delimit complex taxa within the C. sect. Thea.
The discordance between patterns of species resolu­
tion based on nuclear and chloroplast data suggests that 
potential evolutionary processes, such as incomplete lin­
eage sorting (ILS), hybridization and chloroplast capture 
[41, 67, 68], may have shaped the species diversification of

Camellia [22, 41, 63] and thus blurred the species bound­
aries. For example, the phylogenetic analyses revealed 
intriguing insights into the evolutionary relationship 
between C. grandibracteata and C. sinensis var. assamica 
(Fig. 1; Fig. S2). In the nuclear tree the C. grandibracte­
ata samples were monophyletic and nested within the C. 
sinensis var. assamica clade (both in the clade S-IICSA, 
N-IICSA of Fig. 1), whereas in the chloroplast trees, they 
clustered with two accessions of C. sinensis var. assamica, 
potentially indicating past hybridization events between 
these two taxa [29]. Morphological evidence and over­
lapping distribution patterns support a previous hypoth­
esis that C. grandibracteata may be a hybrid between 
C. taliensis and C. sinensis var. assamica [69]. Addition­
ally, gene flow between C. taliensis and C. sinensis var. 
assamica has previously been detected [70, 71], where 
these two species, along with C. grandibracteata, share 
the same flowering period and have the same number 
of somatic chromosomes (2n = 30) [16, 72]. Thus, based 
on our findings and evidence from previous studies, we 
propose that C. grandibracteata should be regarded as a 
homoploid hybrid species.
It was speculated that hybridization between C. 
taliensis and C. sinensis var. assamica has occurred in 
the past [5, 46, 47, 69, 73]. In our study, all ten acces­
sions of C. taliensis formed a single clade in the nuclear 
trees (Fig. 1B and C), while more complex phylogenetic 
relationships were seen in the plastid trees. Four acces­
sions of C. taliensis clustered with the ancient tea tree 
DASZ from Baoshan in a small clade, which was sister 
to another small clade consisting of seven accessions of 
C. sinensis var. assamica. Population genetic analyses 
found gene flow between C. taliensis and C. sinensis var. 
assamica [70, 71, 73]. This pattern further supports that 
C. sinensis var. assamica likely has repeatedly hybridized 
with C. taliensis [5], serving as the maternal parent and 
capturing chloroplasts from C. taliensis. Chloroplast cap­
ture is a common evolutionary phenomenon observed in 
many angiosperm groups [74–76]. Notably, the ancient 
tea tree ‘DASZ’, identified as C. sinensis for genome 
sequencing [42], appeared to be incorrectly named. Our 
results implied that this ancient tea tree may be a hybrid 
progeny of C. taliensis and an ancestor of cultivated C. 
sinensis, with C. taliensis likely its maternal parent. Fur­
thermore, gene flow from C. taliensis into C. sinensis var. 
sinensis and C. sinensis var. assamica has also been docu­
mented [71]. These findings indicate the importance of 
accurate species identification, which should always be 
supported by voucher specimens deposited in a publicly 
accessible herbarium and is also crucial for developmen­
tal and evolutionary studies and breeding research.
Although the C. fangchengensis samples were strongly 
resolved as monophyletic in the chloroplast trees, the two 
accessions of the species grouped in distinct clades in the 
nuclear trees (Fig. 1; Fig. S2). The scattered placements in 
the nuclear trees suggest that hybridization has led to the 
failure of species discrimination via nuclear data. Nota­
bly, gene flow was detected between C. fangchengensis 
and several other species within C. sect. Thea, supporting 
the possibility of historical or ongoing introgression [47]. 
However, more data and analyses are needed to support 
this hypothesis.
Camellia crassicolumna is not clearly delimited in 
either chloroplast or nuclear phylogenies. The four 
samples closely correlated with C. kwangsiensis and C. 
taliensis as a clade in the nuclear trees (Fig. 1; Fig. S2B). 
The individuals scattered in clade pt-I of the chloroplast 
trees indicate an unstable relationship, which aligns with 
previous studies (Fig. 1; Fig. S2) [32, 77–79]. In previous 
work on Camellia or Theaceae, C. crassicolumna was 
found most closely related to other C. sect. Thea species 
(i.e., C. gymnogyna, C. ptilophylla, C. remotiserrata, C. 
tachangensis) [1, 28, 30, 41, 47, 80, 81], suggesting that C. 
crassicolumna may not be a ‘good species’ [32]. Further­
more, shared ancestral components were detected among 
C. crassicolumna, C. taliensis, C. sinensis var. assamica, 
and C. tachangensis, suggesting a complex genetic back­
ground [73]. The samples analyzed here may represent 
hybrid offspring resulting from multiple hybridization 
events among C. sect. Thea species. While previous stud­
ies have reported on such extensive hybridization events 
within C. sect. Thea [47], underscoring the permeability 
of species boundaries within this section species. These 
hypotheses require further verification through popula­
tion genetic sampling and analyses.
Tea plants are known to cross-pollinate and often 
occur sympatrically with overlapping flowering times, 
leading to possible gene flow among species. Conse­
quently, their offspring may exhibit complex genetic, 
physiological or morphological variation [10, 25, 82, 
83], posing challenges for species discrimination. Col­
lectively, the primary reasons for the difficulties in spe­
cies discrimination include the presence of samples likely 
of hybrid origin, introgression and chloroplast capture, 
resulting in species non-monophyly. It is also not surpris­
ing that the two main systems of classification of C. sect. 
Thea [16, 17], which emphasize different structures, such 
as leaves, flowers, and geographic distributions, strongly 
disagree and may not fully capture the complex morphol­
ogy of C. sect. Thea species. The results of the molecu­
lar species delimitation here can be viewed as a draft for 
an advanced taxonomy rather than as the sole criterion 
for species description. To increase the accuracy of spe­
cies delimitation within this group, it is crucial to include 
additional morphologically typical individuals of these 
species from wild populations, particularly from their 
type localities, for further molecular species delimitation 
research.

Treatment of Camellia sinensis varieties
Distinguishing species from cultivated plants is chal­
lenging, particularly because of the lack of unambiguous 
breeding and domestication records. The samples of C. 
sinensis var. sinensis are paraphyletic due to the nesting of 
C. sinensis var. pubilimba (both chloroplast and nuclear 
trees), two individuals with C. sinensis var. lasiocalyx 
located near the base of clade S-IICSA/N-IICSA in the 
nuclear trees, and C. leptophylla (chloroplast tree) within 
clade pt-IIaCSS (Fig.  1; Fig. S2). This can be explained 
by the possibility that the differentiating morphological 
characteristics between C. sinensis var. pubilimba and C. 
sinensis var. sinensis were selected repeatedly and inde­
pendently by breeders throughout the history of tea cul­
tivation [84, 85]. Consequently, we propose treating C. 
sinensis var. pubilimba as a synonym of C. sinensis var. 
sinensis.
In addition, C. sinensis var. assamica was found to be 
monophyletic with high support in the SCN trees (Fig. 1; 
Fig. S2B) but not in the other trees. Interestingly, the core 
accessions of C. sinensis var. sinensis (clade pt-IIaCSS/S-
IICSS/N-IICSS) and C. sinensis var. assamica (pt-IIaCSA/
S-IICSA/N-IICSA) 
formed 
distinct, 
well-supported 
clades in both the chloroplast and the Skmer trees (Fig. 1; 
Fig. S2). Based on morphology, geographic distribution 
and our phylogenomic evidence, we recommend recog­
nizing C. sinensis var. assamica and C. sinensis var. sinen­
sis as separate species, C. assamica (J. W. Mast.) H. T. 
Chang and C. sinensis (L.) Kuntze, respectively, and as 
previously suggested by Chang [86] and Chang and Ren 
[16].
Camellia sinensis var. lasiocalyx, known as Cambod 
tea, with medium-sized leaves was initially cultivated in 
Indo-China and later treated as a synonym of C. sinensis 
var. assamica [17]. Recently, molecular studies have indi­
cated that Cambod tea may be a hybrid between C. assa­
mica and C. sinensis [87]. However, our results showed 
that C. sinensis var. lasiocalyx has close phylogenetic rela­
tionships with C. assamica, C. crassicolumna, C. sinensis 
and C. taliensis, as well as close reticular relationships 
with C. assamica and C. ptilophylla. This might indi­
cate that the parents of C. sinensis var. lasiocalyx (re102, 
re107, re116, re118) are not only cultivated species but 
also other wild relatives (e.g., C. crassicolumna, C. ptilo­
phylla and C. taliensis) (Figs. 1 and 3; Fig. S2).
Overall, with a view to the morphological classifica­
tion system, our study proposes that C. sect. Thea com­
prises at least 14 species: 11 of the 12 species (except C. 
sealyama T. L. Ming) recognized by Ming [17]; C. for­
mosensis (Masam. & Suzuki) M. H. Su, C. F. Hsieh & C. 
H. Tsou [19]; and two further species, C. assamica (J. W. 
Mast.) H. T. Chang [86] and C. remotiserrata H. T. Chang 
[16], both of which are suggested to raise to species status 
strongly supported by our molecular evidence.
Outlook for genomic DNA barcoding in Camellia sect. Thea
The benefits of using chloroplast data for plant species 
identification have been acknowledged in other studies 
[36, 88, 89]. However, for taxonomically complex groups, 
the incorporation of nuclear data has been shown to sig­
nificantly increase species identification accuracy [36]. 
While some studies have attempted to use chloroplast 
data for delimiting species within C. sect. Thea [32], no 
studies to date have combined such analyses with nuclear 
data within this section utilizing multiple samples per 
taxon. In this study, nine of the 14 species (including 11 
species recognized in Ming’s classification and the newly 
recognized species C. formosensis, C. assamica and C. 
remotiserrata) were successfully delimited via the chlo­
roplast alone (Table  1). Notably, two nuclear genome-
based analyses used here (i.e., Skmer analyses based on 
low coverage reads and ML tree reconstructed based on 
759 concatenated SCNs) were employed for the first time 
as genome-wide DNA barcodes for species delimitation 
within C. sect. Thea. Both of our nuclear genome datas­
ets delimited nine out of the 14 species but were not the 
same as those delineated with chloroplast data, and 12 
species were successfully delineated using the combined 
nuclear and chloroplast datasets (Table  1). Removal of 
putative hybrid accessions (i.e., C. sinensis var. pubilimba 
(CE, HZ002, JX4), C. sinensis var. lasiocalyx (re102, re107, 
re116, re118), C. sinensis var. sinensis (re049, W34), and 
C. crassicolumna (re423)), all C. sect. Thea species would 
have been successfully delimitated based on both nuclear 
and chloroplast data, underscoring the application of this 
comprehensive approach for species delimitation within 
C. sect. Thea.
Genome skimming, a relatively cost-effective NGS 
technology that generates approximately 2 Gb of data per 
sample, can be used for chloroplast genome assembly and 
Skmer analyses [35, 36]. However, Skmer analysis, which 
relies on genetic distance matrices, is unable to identify 
the specific sequence regions that contribute to species 
differentiation. Nevertheless, it has demonstrated robust 
discriminatory power across multiple plant groups [35–
37]. In the case of C. sect. Thea, the results from Skmer 
analyses differed from those of SCN; C. kwangsiensis was 
resolved as monophyletic with strong support (BS: 100%) 
based on Skmer analyses, but not in the SCN tree (Fig. 1). 
This result highlights the potential of Skmer as a com­
plementary method of species identification. However, 
assembling large-scale SCNs requires whole genome 
sequencing data with greater coverage (10× − 20× depth), 
which is increasingly utilized in phylogenomic studies [1, 
90–92], as well as in studies on radiative speciation and 
hybridization [74, 93, 94]. In our study, C. sinensis var. 
assamica was found to be monophyletic with high sup­
port (BS: 99%) in the SCN trees (Fig. 1; Fig. S2B) but not 
in the other trees. Therefore, SCNs hold great potential

involved in recent radiation or reticulate evolutionary 
histories [36]. Furthermore, combining both uniparen­
tally inherited chloroplast data and biparentally inher­

delimitation. For example, three species (C. assamica, C. 
grandibracteata and C. taliensis) were delimitated based 
on nuclear genomic data but not on the basis of chloro­
plast data. Conversely, two species (C. fangchengensis and 
C. gymnogyna) were delimitated by chloroplast data but 
not by nuclear genome data. Overall, our findings indi­
cate that chloroplast genome data combined with nuclear 
genome data increases species delimitation among taxo­
nomically complex taxa, especially those where past 
hybridization is suspected.
Conclusion
As an integrated approach to species delimitation, our 
research utilized genome barcodes based on ~ 15× WGS 
data from 98 samples of C. sect. Thea to assemble 759 
single-copy nuclear gene matrices and their whole chlo­
roplast genomes, and 2× coverage of clean WGS reads 
for Skmer analysis. Our study provides novel insights 
into species delimitation within C. sect. Thea, clarifying 
the taxonomic position of previously controversial spe­
cies due to their minor morphological differences. Two 
taxa are proposed to be elevated to species level, C. assa­
mica and C. remotiserrata. We further found that com­
bining results from chloroplast and nuclear genome data 
increased the level of species delimitation. Our study has 
significantly enhanced our understanding of the taxa in 
C. sect. Thea, and ultimately allowed the proposal of 14 
species in this section. The findings will prove invaluable 
for the development of taxonomy, future conservation 
strategies and breeding efforts involving cultivated tea 
plants and their wild relatives.

Abstract: Background Species delimitation within Camellia sect. Thea is taxonomically challenging due to its complex evolutionary history. This study aims to utilize nuclear and chloroplast data as genomic DNA barcodes to delimit species within this economically important group of plants. Results Whole genome sequencing (WGS) data were obtained for 98 accessions representing all but one species in C. sect. Thea. Based on 759 high-quality SCNs, 98 whole chloroplast genomes, and by using 2× coverage clean reads from WGS for Skmer analyses, we found that combining the findings from these three data sets resulted in nearly complete species delimitation and resolution of all interspecific relationships within C. sect. Thea. We also found support for the taxonomic elevation of two varieties (C. sinensis var. assamica and C. tachangensis var. remotiserrata) to species status (C. assamica and C. remotiserrata, respectively). Furthermore, we confirmed that C. formosensis represents a distinct species. Gene tree discordances, chloroplast-nuclear conflicts and complex network-like phylogenetic relationships were observed in C. sect. Thea. Conclusion Compared with the use of single parentally inherited chloroplast data sources, utilizing both uniparentally inherited chloroplast data and biparentally inherited nuclear data improved the species delimitation of taxa within C. sect. Thea. The intricate phylogenetic relationships observed are likely a result of widespread past hybridization and chloroplast capture events among species within this group, which may have blurred the species boundaries. Our novel approach to species delimitation within C. sect. Thea may serve as a blueprint for employing genomic DNA barcodes in other taxa with complex histories, and will significantly contribute to the conservation of cultivated tea plant species and their wild relatives.
